newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's Suharto pledges further deregulation.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Suharto pledges further deregulation.

text.p: Indonesia's President Suharto on Tuesday pledged to further deregulate the fast-growing economy while ordering his ministers to crack down on corruption.
Information Minister Harmoko quoted Suharto as telling a cabinet meeting that steps had to be taken to ease government red tape and to continue with the privatisation of state firms.

"The president asked the coordinating economic minister to increase coordination of deregulation measures that have to be taken," Harmoko told reporters after the cabinet meeting that discussed the 1997/98 (April/March) state budget.

"Steps need to be taken to overcome the complicated bureaucratic chain, to simplify procedures...in issuing business licences, to simplify customs procedures and to create a consistent business climate," Harmoko quoted Suharto as saying.
Suharto also said that government funds must be accounted for.
"The administration of state finance must be implemented orderly," Suharto was quoted as saying.
"Ministers must work with the coordinating economic minister to take firm and fast action against symptoms of deviation, leakage, extravagance and corruption," Suharto said.
He also ordered the finance minister to continue privatising state firms by listing them on international stock exchanges.

"We have succeeded in listing shares of state-owned companies on international stock exchanges. Following that success, the president instructed the privatisation of more state companies by listing their shares abroad," Harmoko said.

Indonesia has listed state firms such as PT Indonesian Satellite Corporation (Indosat) and PT Telekomunikasi Indonesia (Telkom) in New York. Telkom is also listed in London, along with miner PT Tambang Timah.

Harmoko said Suharto also instructed the monetary authority to implement prudent fiscal and monetary policies aimed at preventing economic overheating, a widening in the current account deficit and containing inflation.
Planning Minister Ginanjar Kartasasmita said on Saturday Indonesia had a healthy economic outlook for 1997, with growth estimated at 7.9 percent and inflation at around six percent.
He said the economy was expected to grow by between 7.6 and 7.9 percent this year, while inflation was seen at between 6.5 and 6.8 percent.

Indonesia has estimated its current account deficit will widen to $8.7 billion in fiscal 1996/97 (April-March), or about four percent of gross domestic product (GDP), from $7.0 billion, or about 3.2 percent of GDP, in 1995/96.

"The president also asked the finance minister and the Central Bank governor to increase supervision of banks, insurance companies and pension funds to ensure funds are used in an efficient and effective way," Harmoko said.
